opus-5.5.text:
I think AlphaProof was a real milestone, and maybe not for the reason most headlines focused on. The headline was "AI gets silver-medal level at the IMO," which is exciting. But for me the deeper significance was *how* it got there.

AlphaProof worked in Lean, a formal proof language. Every proof it produced could be checked by a computer, line by line. That's very different from a language model writing something that *looks* like a proof, where you then need a human expert to read it and decide whether it's correct. With formal verification you get a ground-truth signal, and once you have that, you can do reinforcement learning the way AlphaGo did for Go. The system tries things, the verifier says right or wrong, and it improves from that feedback at scale. To me, that was the proof of concept that mathematics can become a domain like Go, where self-play and search actually work.

It also showed the bottlenecks very honestly. Some problems took the system up to a few days of compute, far beyond the time a human contestant gets. The problems were translated into Lean by humans first. And it struggled with the combinatorics problems, which tend to be the hardest to formalize and the most dependent on clever, informal insight. So it wasn't "AI has solved math." It was "here is a path that works, and here are the walls you'll hit along it."

I'd say three things came out of it. First, autoformalization, turning natural-language math into formal statements, is a central problem, not a side problem. Second, data scarcity in formal math is severe. There's very little Lean compared to the amount of informal math on the internet, so you have to generate your own data, essentially bootstrapping. Third, competition math is a stepping stone, not the destination. IMO problems are self-contained and have known answers. Research mathematics means building new definitions, new theories, and long chains of lemmas. That's a much bigger leap.

So I see AlphaProof as the "AlphaGo moment" for formal math. It made a lot of people, including me, believe that combining language models with formal verification and RL is the right architecture for building something like an AI mathematician. The open question since then has been how to scale it from olympiad problems to real research, and that's honestly what gets me up in the morning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think AlphaProof was a genuine milestone, and I want to be precise about why, because people tend to either overhype it or dismiss it.

What DeepMind did was take the International Mathematical Olympiad problems, formalize them in Lean, and then have a system that combined a language model with AlphaZero-style reinforcement learning search through the space of proofs. Together with AlphaGeometry 2, it solved four of the six problems, which is silver medal level. The important part isn't the medal, it's the method. Lean gives you a verifier. Every step of the proof is checked by the kernel, so there's no hallucination problem in the usual sense. The model can be wrong a million times during search, and that's fine, because only a verified proof counts. That turns mathematics into something much closer to Go: a domain where you can generate your own training signal through self-play, and where the reward is unambiguous.

That's the piece I find most consequential. For years the bottleneck for AI in math was data. There are very few formal proofs in the world compared to, say, lines of Python. AlphaProof showed a path around that: autoformalize a huge number of informal problems, then let the system attempt them and learn from the ones it gets right. It's a flywheel, and it's the same flywheel that worked in games.

Now the caveats, which I think matter. First, the problems had to be formalized by humans before the system could attack them. Autoformalization of statements is still hard, and it's harder for research-level mathematics where even stating the theorem cleanly is part of the work. Second, the compute was enormous. One of the problems reportedly took something like three days, and an IMO contestant has four and a half hours. So it wasn't a fair fight in terms of resources, and that's fine as a proof of concept, but it tells you we're not yet at efficient reasoning. Third, olympiad problems are a particular kind of mathematics. They're self-contained, they have short, clever solutions, and the answer is known to exist. Research mathematics is open-ended. You don't know if the conjecture is true, you don't know which definitions are the right ones, and much of the value is in building theory rather than closing a single problem.

So my read is: AlphaProof settled the question of whether machines can do serious, verified mathematical reasoning. The answer is yes. What it didn't settle is whether they can do mathematics the way mathematicians actually do it, which is cumulative, conceptual, and mostly about choosing the right questions. That's where I think the next few years of work lie, and it's a big part of why I'm excited about building in this space. The verifier is the key insight. Once you have a reliable verifier, scaling does a lot of the rest, and Lean plus a strong model is the first real demonstration of that in a domain humans actually care about.

astra-6.text:
I see it as an important milestone, but I’d distinguish between solving a difficult mathematical problem and doing mathematical research. A system that can find a proof is demonstrating something valuable. But research also involves deciding which questions to ask, forming useful definitions, and recognizing why a result matters.

What excites me is the possibility of bringing those capabilities together: AI that helps mathematicians explore ideas, while giving us proofs we can check rigorously. So I’d view AlphaProof as an encouraging step toward that future, rather than evidence that the whole process of mathematical discovery has been solved.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as an important milestone, especially because it connects mathematical reasoning with formal verification. With a system like AlphaProof, the goal isn’t just to produce an argument that sounds convincing; it’s to produce a proof that can be checked precisely.

But I would distinguish success on competition problems from doing mathematical research. In research, you also have to decide which questions are interesting, formulate useful definitions, and develop concepts when you don’t yet know what the destination should be. Solving a clearly stated problem is one part of that process.

So I’m excited about what this suggests for collaboration between mathematicians and AI. The opportunity is to help us explore ideas and verify difficult steps, while gradually expanding the kinds of mathematical reasoning these systems can handle.
